title: Money Tray
context: Grade 4, the chapter's first section, on notes and coins. An adult sees notes and coins being sorted, which a table top does perfectly well. What is actually being settled is that money is counted by value and not by pieces: six coins can be worth less than one note, and many notes of one value are counted by multiplying before any groups are added. The printed exercise then asks whether some money is enough when it is exactly enough, and who has more money when both have the same. Exactly enough is enough, and when two amounts are equal neither is more. This tool shows every note and coin by its value alone.

writeup.why: Sort notes and coins by their value, count each group by multiplying, add the groups, and decide whether the total is enough or which amount is more.
writeup.look: A counting tray of value slots across the canvas, a heap of notes and coins above it, a sum rail along its foot, and a price card with an enough gauge at the right.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Money Tray' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the pieces sorted against the pieces in the heap, two numbers in ink, the first climbing by one as each note or coin settles in its slot and the second fixed at the size of the heap. On the second phase it carries the notes counted against the notes in the slot, and on the third and fourth the groups added against the groups filled. Nothing in it ever counts down and nothing in it ever reads as a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. The heap lies across the top of the working area, 700 by 96 at 64,214, every piece separate and none overlapping. The tray stands under it, 700 by 280 at 64,322, as two rows of value slots, each slot 110 by 128: notes of ten, twenty, fifty, one hundred, two hundred and five hundred rupees along the top row, and coins of one, two, five, ten and twenty rupees along the bottom, each slot labelled with its value in deep blue. A piece dropped in settles only in the slot for its value; dropped anywhere else it slides back to the heap with its value lit. A slot shows up to ten pieces fanned, and past ten it ties them in stacks of ten with a near-black band, so twenty-seven coins read as two tied stacks and seven loose. Under each filled slot a small group card gives the count in sky blue and the group's amount in deep blue, and tapping it opens the group reader, a strip 700 by 44 at 64,606, which writes the whole line: seven notes of two hundred rupees, seven times two hundred, make one thousand four hundred rupees. The sum rail runs along the foot, 700 by 60 at 64,660, taking each group's amount as a deep blue bar drawn to one scale, laid end to end, with the running total written at its right hand end; it takes a group's amount and never its count. At the right, the price card stands 370 by 88 at 780,214, and the enough gauge under it, 370 by 250 at 780,318, lays the total as a deep blue bar under the price's bar, both starting from one near-black line and drawn to the same scale. The gauge reads short when the total's bar stops before the price's end, exactly enough when the two ends meet, and more than enough when it runs past. The second tray folds out under the gauge, 370 by 150 at 780,580, holding another amount as its own groups; with two trays out, the gauge lays the two totals as two bars and reads which holds more, or neither when their ends meet. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve number keys three across wherever an amount or a count is asked for, with a unit tag under the slot reading rupees, filled in beside the number and never left off. On the first phase a word pad sits over it with a key for each of the two lots being compared and a key reading the same, and on the fourth it carries keys reading short, exactly enough, more than enough and neither. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own and are the pictures' colours too. The rupees of every amount, the rupees column and the value printed on every note and coin are deep blue. The paise of every amount, the paise column and every cell standing for paise are green. The dot between rupees and paise is vermilion, a clear round dot, and wherever amounts stand in columns it sits on a near-black dotted line. A rupee carried from the paise, and a rupee broken into a hundred paise with the digits it rewrites, are amber. The change handed back, the money left and a remainder are reddish purple, so money coming back is never mistaken for a cost. A count of things, a number multiplied by, how many notes of one value or how many can be bought, is sky blue, because a count of things is not money. The zeros that fill the paise column of a whole-rupee amount in column working are grey. Every play note is one plain pale blue rectangle and every play coin one plain steel disc, all notes one size and all coins one size, each printed with its value and nothing else. No coin below one rupee is drawn anywhere: paise are shaded cells on a strip ruled into a hundred in ten blocks of ten, so a full strip is exactly one rupee. Chrome never borrows one of those and none of them is ever used for chrome: every column rule, dotted line, tick, bracket, strike line, bill rule and panel edge is near-black. Every reading survives with the colour taken away, because a digit is told apart by the column it stands in, a carry by the circle it sits in, a count by the box beside the times sign or the slot marked things, and the change or money left by the tray or line that holds it, before any of them is told by a colour. Grey never means faint: a zero in a paise column is drawn at the same size and weight as every other digit and is never dimmed, shrunk or left out. A rupees figure that goes down by one is struck through once with the new figure written above it, and never rubbed out. The gauge's bars are drawn to one scale for the value of the money and never for the number of pieces, so a heap of many small coins can make a short bar and one note a long one. Stacks of ten are tied only inside a slot, where every piece has one value.
writeup.finish: The card shows the tray the child filled, each group's count and amount under its slot, the total on the sum rail, and the gauge's last reading.

phases.win: every piece sits in its own slot, and the larger amount glows, on the note or on the coins
phases.does: sorts every piece into the slot for its value, then sets one note beside a handful of coins and decides which is worth more
phases.goal: each note and coin is worth the value printed on it, and more pieces need not mean more money
phases.says: Put each piece in the slot for its value. Which is worth more, the one note or the coins?
phases.check: Away from the screen: which is more money, five coins of two rupees or one note of twenty rupees?
phases.feels: the printed value decides, and neither the number of pieces nor paper against metal does
phases.hands: Tip a class bank of play notes and coins onto a desk and sort it by the value printed on each piece. Then hold up one note of fifty rupees in one hand and eight coins of five rupees in the other, and ask which hand holds more money. Count the coins in fives aloud and set them beside the note.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the answer. First rung, from the item's own miss line: what value is printed on each piece? Second rung, the phase's: what is the whole handful worth? Third rung: the heap is cut to one note and two coins, and the child finds what the coins make before the larger heap comes back. The word pad and the number pad stay open behind all three rungs.

wrong.why: a bigger handful looks like more money, and counting pieces is quicker than reading values.
wrong.move: chooses the purse with six coins of ten rupees over the one with a single note of one hundred, because it holds more pieces.
wrong.screen: the six coins drop into the ten rupee slot and the note into the hundred rupee slot, and the group card under the coins reads six coins of ten rupees making sixty rupees. The gauge lays both lots as bars from one line, and the coins' bar stops well short of the note's. The child's choice stays lit on the word pad, nothing marked.

wrong.why: on this tray the notes run up to five hundred and the coins stop at twenty, so paper looks worth more than metal whatever is printed on it.
wrong.move: says a note of ten rupees is worth more than a coin of twenty rupees, because it is a note.
wrong.screen: both pieces drop into their slots, the coin into the slot marked twenty and the note into the slot marked ten, and their printed values light in deep blue. The gauge lays the coin's bar twice as long as the note's, and the child's choice stays on the word pad beside it.

phases.screen: a small heap of notes and coins tipped out above the empty tray
phases.soWhat: Each note and coin is worth the value printed on it. A coin and a note of the same value are worth the same.
phases.concept: The value of each note and coin

phases.win: the reader writes the count times the value, and the group's amount glows under the slot
phases.does: counts the notes, multiplies by their value, and writes the group's amount
phases.goal: many notes of one value are counted by multiplying the number of notes by the value
phases.says: How many notes are there, and what is each one worth? How much is the whole group?
phases.check: How much money is twelve notes of twenty rupees? Say the count and the value first.
phases.feels: a group of one value is that value again and again, so the count says how many times
phases.hands: Give each group a bundle of eight notes of fifty rupees. Count the notes, then lay them down one at a time while the class says the running total in fifties. Write eight times fifty beside the last total, and ask why the two agree.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: how many notes are in the slot? Second rung, the phase's: what is each one worth? Third rung: the slot is cut to three notes, laid down one at a time along the rail, before the larger group comes back. The number pad stays open.

wrong.why: two numbers stand in the question, and adding is the first thing to try with two numbers.
wrong.move: adds nine and fifty and writes fifty-nine rupees for nine notes of fifty.
wrong.screen: the group reader lays the nine notes along the sum rail one at a time, each adding a bar of fifty, and the running total climbs fifty, one hundred, one hundred and fifty, and on to four hundred and fifty. The child's fifty-nine is drawn as a bar beside the rail and ends partway along the second note. The child's number stays in the slot.

wrong.why: counting the notes is the first thing done, and it feels like the answer to how much.
wrong.move: answers nine, the number of notes, when the question asks for the money.
wrong.screen: the group card under the slot lights its count, nine, in sky blue, and the unit tag under the answer slot lights rupees in deep blue beside the child's nine. The reader then writes nine notes of fifty rupees, nine times fifty, make four hundred and fifty rupees, and the child's nine stays in the slot.

phases.screen: one slot holding several notes of one value, with its group reader empty
phases.soWhat: Many notes of one value are counted by multiplying the number of notes by the value.
phases.concept: Counting a group of one note

phases.win: the running total grows with each group and settles at the end of the rail
phases.does: reads each group's amount and slides the groups onto the sum rail one at a time
phases.goal: a total is found by working out each group's value first and then adding the groups
phases.says: Find what each group is worth first. Then add the groups together.
phases.check: Find the total of four notes of fifty rupees, three coins of ten rupees and two coins of two rupees.
phases.feels: a group is only ready to add once its count has been turned into rupees
phases.hands: Fill an envelope with three notes of one hundred rupees, five notes of ten rupees and four coins of two rupees. Groups sort it, write each group's value on a slip, and only then add the slips. Ask what the slips would have said if the pieces had been counted without looking at their values.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: what is the first group worth? Second rung, the phase's: has every group been turned into rupees? Third rung: the tray is cut to two groups, and the child finds each amount before sliding either onto the rail. The number pad stays open.

wrong.why: the values are the numbers printed large on the slots, and the counts under them are easy to leave behind.
wrong.move: adds one of each value, two hundred, twenty and five, and writes Rs 225, as if each group held one piece.
wrong.screen: the group cards light their counts in sky blue, three, four and six, and each group slides onto the sum rail whole: six hundred, then eighty, then thirty, the total climbing to seven hundred and ten. The child's two hundred and twenty-five is laid as a bar beside the rail, ending partway along the first group, and the child's number stays in the slot.

wrong.why: the counts are the numbers the child made while sorting, and adding what was just counted feels like finishing the job.
wrong.move: adds the counts, three, four and six, and writes thirteen rupees.
wrong.screen: the sum rail refuses the sky blue counts: each one slides up to the rail and back to its card. The thirteen pieces are then lit in their slots, three notes of two hundred, four notes of twenty and six coins of five, three different values, and each group's amount goes onto the rail in deep blue instead. The child's thirteen stays in the slot beside the total.

phases.screen: three or four slots filled with groups of different values, and the sum rail empty
phases.soWhat: Find what each group is worth first, then add the groups.

phases.win: the gauge settles on its reading, and two equal trays sit level with neither more
phases.does: finds the total, lays it against the price and reads the gauge, then sets two trays side by side and says which holds more
phases.goal: a total is compared with a price or with another amount, exactly enough is enough, and when two amounts are the same neither is more
phases.says: Is the money short of the price, exactly enough, or more?
phases.check: One friend has four notes of fifty rupees and another has ten notes of twenty rupees. Who has more money?
phases.feels: the gauge does not care how the money is made up, only how far its bar reaches
phases.hands: Write a price of three hundred rupees on a card. Give one group exactly three hundred rupees in mixed play money, another two hundred and eighty and a third three hundred and fifty, and each group says short, exactly enough or more than enough. Then give two groups the same amount in different notes, and ask which has more.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: what is the total? Second rung, the phase's: where does the total's bar end against the price's? Third rung: the tray is cut to one note laid against a price card of the same value, and the child reads the gauge before the larger tray comes back. The word pad and the number pad stay open.

wrong.why: enough can sound like having some to spare, and a purse emptied to nothing feels like falling short.
wrong.move: says no, the money is not enough, because nothing will be left over after paying three hundred and fifty rupees.
wrong.screen: the gauge lays the total, three hundred and fifty rupees, under the price's bar, and the two ends meet at the same mark with no gap and no overhang. The gauge's word settles on exactly enough, the key reading exactly enough lights on the pad, and the child's no stays where it was pressed.

wrong.why: a handful of six pieces looks like plenty, and counting the pieces is quicker than adding their values.
wrong.move: decides six pieces must be enough for a book of two hundred and fifty rupees, without finding their total.
wrong.screen: the two notes of one hundred and the four coins of ten go into their slots, the rail adds two hundred and forty, and the gauge lays that bar under the price's. It stops ten rupees short of the price's end, the gap bracketed in near-black, and the child's answer stays on the pad beside it.

wrong.why: the question asks who has more, which sounds as though one of them must, and sixteen notes are more notes.
wrong.move: names the child with sixteen notes of one hundred rupees as having more money than the child with eight notes of two hundred.
wrong.screen: both trays fold out and the gauge lays two bars, one thousand six hundred rupees each, whose ends meet at the same mark. The gauge's word turns to neither, the key reading neither lights, and the child's choice stays on the pad beside it.

phases.screen: a filled tray with a price card beside it, the enough gauge waiting, and a second tray ready
phases.soWhat: Exactly enough is enough, and when two amounts are the same, neither is more.

writeup.delight: The fourth phase, when a tray of eight notes of two hundred rupees is set against a tray of sixteen notes of one hundred. The two bars grow on the gauge side by side and their ends meet exactly. Then the notes themselves move: each note of two hundred rupees slides out, and two notes of one hundred rupees from the other tray pair up beside it, eight pairs in a row with not one note left over on either side, and the gauge's word turns to neither. It can be tried with any two trays as often as a finger likes, nothing is marked, and the voice says nothing at all while it happens.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. On the first phase a small heap of notes and coins lies tipped out above the empty tray. On the second one slot already holds a group of notes of one value, with its group card blank. On the third three or four slots hold groups of different values, and the sum rail along the foot is empty. On the fourth a filled tray stands with a price card beside it and the enough gauge at rest, and a second tray waits folded under the gauge. The running count at the top left holds the pieces sorted against the pieces in the heap, and the answer slot and the pad stand empty down the right. One thing moves, once: the heap, or the filled slot, or the first group, or the price card, gives one slow pulse while the voice asks what each piece is worth. That pulse is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any heap of notes and coins, with the group reader, the sum rail and the enough gauge open. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on the value of each note and coin, counting a group by multiplying, adding the groups, and deciding whether a total is enough or which amount is more.
voiceLines: A heap of notes and coins and a row of slots. What is each piece worth?
Put each piece in the slot for its value. Which is worth more, the one note or the coins?
How many notes are there, and what is each one worth? How much is the whole group?
Find what each group is worth first. Then add the groups together.
Is the money short of the price, exactly enough, or more?
A new heap. Sort it by value before you count anything.
Free play. Any heap, with the reader, the rail and the gauge open.
Read the value on each piece again, and count the group, not the pile.
Every piece in its slot, every group counted, and every total laid against the price.

observations.why: The bar is drawn for value, and six coins of ten rupees are worth sixty rupees while the note is worth a hundred.
observations.soWhat: Money is counted by value, not by pieces, so more pieces need not mean more money.
observations.observe: The six coins made a shorter bar on the gauge than the one note.

observations.why: Every note in the slot has the same value, so the group is that value again for each note.
observations.soWhat: Many notes of one value are counted by multiplying the number of notes by the value.
observations.observe: The group reader wrote the count beside the value, and the amount matched laying the value down that many times.

observations.why: Counts of different notes are counts of different things, but their amounts are all rupees.
observations.soWhat: Find what each group is worth first, then add the groups.
observations.observe: The sum rail took each group's amount, and would not take a count.

observations.why: The same amount covers the price with nothing short, and two equal amounts leave neither one ahead.
observations.soWhat: Exactly enough is enough, and when two amounts are the same, neither is more.
observations.observe: When the two ends met, the gauge read exactly enough, and two equal trays read neither.

description: Sort notes and coins by the value printed on them, count a group of one value by multiplying, add the groups to a total, and lay the total against a price or another amount.

serves.exercise: finding how much money a five hundred and a two hundred rupee note make with two notes each of one hundred and fifty rupees
finding the total amount of each of three sets of notes and coins
finding how much money a wallet of two hundred, five hundred and one hundred rupee notes holds
deciding whether the notes and coins taken for a picnic make the five hundred rupees asked for

source_tool.description: A counting tray fills the stage with a row of slots, one for each value: notes of ten, twenty, fifty, one hundred, two hundred and five hundred rupees, and coins of one, two, five, ten and twenty rupees. Every note and coin shows its value in large figures and nothing else. A heap of mixed money is tipped out above the tray, and a piece dropped in settles only in the slot for its value; a piece dropped in the wrong slot slides back with its value lit. Under each filled slot a group reader writes the count, the value and what they make together, such as seven notes of two hundred rupees making one thousand four hundred rupees. A sum rail along the foot of the tray takes the group amounts one at a time into a running total. On the right, a price card or a second tray can be set beside the first. An enough gauge lays the total against the price and reads short, exactly enough or more than enough, or, for two trays, says which holds more, and reads neither when the two totals are the same.
source_tool.art_direction: Notes and coins sorted into value slots / Picture book

audio.note: Web Audio oscillators, no files. The same three cues in every tool of every Class 4 chapter, so the grade sounds like one grade.

wrong.note: A soft low double-bloop. A nudge, never a buzzer.

modes.freePlay: Out of scope here. It is not reached from inside a phase mount, because a phase mount ends idle and has no finish card to reach it from. writeup.freePlay stays as the record of what that activity is, for whoever builds it as its own thing.

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: a rupee tray and a paise tray, strips ruled into a hundred cells, a counting tray of value slots, a bill slip with a dotted line, a shop counter with a change tray, a multiplying frame under a row of things, and a till with a share mat.

Every note and coin shows its value in large figures and nothing else: no design, no picture, no lettering but the value. Every note is a plain paper rectangle and every coin a plain metal disc, all notes one size and one colour and all coins one size and one metal, so a value is read from its print and never from size or colour.

No coin below one rupee is drawn or named anywhere. Wherever paise are drawn rather than written, they are shaded cells on a rupee strip ruled into a hundred equal cells in ten blocks of ten, so a full strip is exactly one rupee. Nothing standing for paise is ever round.

Written money with paise is Rs, the rupees, a dot and two digits of paise, as Rs 96.75. Fewer than ten paise are written with a zero in the first place after the dot. A whole amount in running text is written with no dot, as Rs 43.

Column working always stands on a dotted line: every dot in a column sits on it, rupees to its left and paise to its right. In column working a whole-rupee amount carries two zeros in its paise column, drawn at the same size and weight as every other digit.

A hundred paise rolling up into one rupee is always shown moving, from the paise column into a small carry circle over the rupees, and a rupee broken into paise is always shown opening into a full strip of a hundred cells.
A rupees figure that goes down by one is struck through and the new figure written above it, never erased, so the break can be read afterwards.
The number of things in a product is a count. It stands in a box of its own beside the times sign, outside the rupees and paise columns, with no dot, and no cell exists for it under the paise.
Every answer slot carries its unit, rupees or things, printed beside the number.
A total, a change, a cost or an amount left is told apart by the slot or line it sits in first and by its colour second, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a digit, a note, a coin, a cell or a slot the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. These are the chapter's own colours, taken from the pictures, so a tool and a picture of the same thing are the same colour. The rupees of every amount, the rupees column and the value printed on every note and coin are deep blue, and the paise of every amount, the paise column and every cell standing for paise are green. The dot between rupees and paise is vermilion in every tool, drawn as a clear round dot on the dotted line. A rupee carried from the paise, and a rupee broken into a hundred paise with the digits it rewrites, are amber. The change handed back, the money left and a remainder are reddish purple, so money coming back is never mistaken for a cost. A count of things, a number multiplied by, how many notes of one value or how many can be bought, is sky blue, because a count is never money. The two zeros in the paise column of a whole-rupee amount are grey, drawn at the same size and weight as every other digit and never faded. Every play note is one plain pale blue and every play coin one plain steel, so a value is read from its print and never from its colour. All of that holds in greyscale, because a digit is told apart by the column it stands in, a carry by the circle it sits in and a count by the box beside the times sign, before any of them is told apart by colour.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Read the value on each piece again, and count the group, not the pile.
voice.onNext: A new heap. Sort it by value before you count anything.
voice.opening: A heap of notes and coins and a row of slots. What is each piece worth?
voice.onFinish: Every piece in its slot, every group counted, and every total laid against the price.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Any heap, with the reader, the rail and the gauge open.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

phase_map.concept: The value of each note and coin
Counting a group of one note

placement.where: After a class bank of play notes and coins has been sorted by value on the desks and each group counted aloud. The tool is what writes each group's count and value together and lays a total against a price, so exactly enough and neither more are seen rather than argued.

answer_key.rule: Every note and coin is worth the value printed on it, and money is counted by value, not by the number of pieces; a coin and a note of the same value are worth the same. Many notes or coins of one value are counted by multiplying the number of pieces by the value. The total of a mix is found by working out each group's value and adding the groups. A total is then compared with a price: less is short, the same is exactly enough, and more is more than enough, and exactly enough counts as enough. When two amounts are the same, neither is more.
answer_key.wrong: The pieces are lifted back out of the tray and dropped in again one slot at a time, each group reader writing its count, value and amount while the sum rail refills. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: Money is counted by value, not by the number of pieces.
Six coins of Rs 10 are worth 6 times 10, which is Rs 60.
One note of Rs 100 is worth Rs 100, and 100 is more than 60.
items.answer: The purse with the Rs 100 note, because six Rs 10 coins make only Rs 60
items.question: One purse holds a Rs 100 note. Another holds six Rs 10 coins. Which purse has more money?
items.checkpoint: Each note and coin is worth the value printed on it; more pieces need not mean more money.
items.misconception: Choosing the purse with six coins because it holds more pieces.

steps: All nine notes have the same value, Rs 50.
Many notes of one value are counted by multiplying: 9 times 50.
9 times 50 is 450, so the group is Rs 450.
items.question: How much money is 9 notes of Rs 50?
items.checkpoint: Many notes of one value are counted by multiplying the number of notes by the value.
items.misconception: Adding 9 and 50 to get 59, or answering 9 because there are nine notes.

steps: Find each group's value: 3 notes of Rs 200 make Rs 600.
4 notes of Rs 20 make Rs 80, and 6 coins of Rs 5 make Rs 30.
Add the groups: 600, 80 and 30 make Rs 710.
items.question: A cash box holds 3 notes of Rs 200, 4 notes of Rs 20 and 6 coins of Rs 5. How much money is in it?
items.checkpoint: Find each group's value first, then add the groups.
items.misconception: Adding one of each value, 200, 20 and 5, to get Rs 225, and forgetting how many there are of each.

steps: Find the total first: Rs 200, then 5 times 20 is Rs 100, and 10 times 5 is Rs 50.
The price is Rs 350 and the money is Rs 350, so it is exactly enough, with nothing left over.
items.answer: Yes, exactly enough. The money comes to Rs 350, the same as the price
items.question: A class trip costs Rs 350. A child brings one Rs 200 note, five Rs 20 notes and ten Rs 5 coins. Is that enough?
items.checkpoint: Find the total, then compare it with the price; exactly enough counts as enough.
items.misconception: Saying no because nothing will be left over, when exactly enough is enough.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: Which is worth more, a Rs 20 coin or a Rs 10 note?
items.final_answer: The Rs 20 coin. A coin or a note is worth the value printed on it

items.question: Which is more money, eight Rs 2 coins or one Rs 20 note?
items.final_answer: The Rs 20 note. Eight Rs 2 coins make only Rs 16

items.question: How much is 14 notes of Rs 500?
A money box holds 27 coins of Rs 5. How much money is that?
Find the total: one Rs 200 note, one Rs 50 note, three Rs 20 notes and three Rs 10 notes.
items.final_answer: Rs 340. The groups are Rs 200, Rs 50, Rs 60 and Rs 30

items.question: A book costs Rs 250. A child has two Rs 100 notes and four Rs 10 coins. Is that enough?
items.final_answer: No. The money comes to Rs 240, which is Rs 10 short of the price

items.question: A box holds 60 coins. Half of them are Rs 10 coins and the rest are Rs 2 coins. How much money is in the box?
items.final_answer: Rs 360. Thirty coins of Rs 10 make Rs 300 and thirty coins of Rs 2 make Rs 60. The question asks for money, not coins

items.question: One child has 8 notes of Rs 200. Another has 16 notes of Rs 100. Who has more money?

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

student_controls.effect: tips out a mix of notes and coins above the tray
take each piece only in the slot for its value
writes a slot's count, its value and what they make together
adds the group amounts one at a time into a running total
sets a price beside the tray
sets another amount beside the first to compare
reads short, exactly enough or more, or which tray holds more, and neither when the two are the same

teaching_notes: Tip a class bank of play notes and coins onto the desks before the tool is opened, sort it by value, and count each group aloud. Then use the tool for what the desk cannot hold still: each group's count and value written together, and a total laid against a price. Teach every note and coin by the value printed on it and nothing else. The chapter lists its notes and coins in a table of designs with a paragraph on which older ones are still accepted, and the opening box says who puts the notes out and whose picture they all carry. None of that is mathematics, some of it is out of date, and this plan does not repeat it. Two exercise questions need a word said. One asks whether a child carried enough money when the total is exactly the price: exactly enough is enough. The other asks which of two children had more money when both had the same: the answer is neither. The On Your Own box can be read three ways. Read it as the book's own answer does, one note each of five hundred and two hundred rupees and two notes each of one hundred and fifty rupees.
generation_prompt: Build a money counting tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. A tray runs across the working area as a row of slots, one per value: notes of ten, twenty, fifty, one hundred, two hundred and five hundred rupees, and coins of one, two, five, ten and twenty rupees. Every note and coin shows only its value in large figures, a note as a plain rectangle and a coin as a plain disc, all notes one size and all coins one size, with nothing else printed on them. A heap of mixed pieces is tipped out above the tray; a piece dropped in settles only in the slot for its value, and a piece dropped in the wrong slot slides back with its value lit, with nothing marked. Under each filled slot a group reader writes the count, the value and the amount they make. A sum rail along the foot of the tray takes the group amounts one at a time into a running total. At the right, a price card or a second tray can be set, and an enough gauge reads short, exactly enough or more than enough, or which tray holds more, reading neither when the two totals are the same. No coin below one rupee appears anywhere. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Put each note and coin in the slot for its value. Multiply to count a group. Add the groups. Lay the total against the price.
